lesson_headings.1: LESSON — Module 1: Your body in space
lesson_headings.2: LESSON — Module 2: Life aboard the orbital station

mission_heading_template: MISSION — Module {N}. Use your training to handle each situation. There is no time limit.

tasks.title: Back on Earth
tasks.situation: Two days after landing from a six-month mission, the flight surgeon measures your height. What will they most likely find?

options.text: About your height before launch — on Earth, gravity presses the spine back together.
You are still several centimeters taller — height gained as an adult stays.
You are shorter than before launch — space shrinks the bones.

tasks.title: After the mission
tasks.situation: You land after a long stay in orbit. When should your favourite food start to taste normal again?

options.text: Within days, once body fluids move back down and your nose clears.
Only after months, as the taste buds slowly recover.
Never fully — spaceflight permanently changes the sense of taste.

tasks.title: Fixing the puffy face
tasks.situation: Which of these would do most to reduce an astronaut's puffy face in orbit?

options.text: A suit that gently pulls blood and fluid down toward the legs.
Eating less salt.
Sleeping in a warmer cabin.

tasks.title: Protecting your bones
tasks.situation: Which daily routine would best protect the bones of your hips and spine during a six-month mission?

options.text: Heavy resistance exercise that loads the legs and spine.
Taking calcium tablets every day.
Spending more time near the windows for sunlight.

tasks.title: A breeze in the lab
tasks.situation: In the station lab, a small fan blows air steadily across a candle flame. What will the flame most likely look like?

options.text: Stretched out in the direction the air is flowing.
Perfectly round and blue, as always in orbit.
Green, because of the fan's electric motor.

tasks.title: A drop on your fingertip
tasks.situation: In orbit, you hold your finger pointing "down" with a drop of water on its tip. What happens?

options.text: The drop stays on your finger — nothing pulls it away.
It drips off, just a little more slowly than on Earth.
It freezes into ice.

tasks.title: A higher station
tasks.situation: A future station circles Earth in a higher orbit, taking 180 minutes per orbit. About how many sunrises will its crew see in 24 hours?

options.text: About 8
About 16, the same as on the ISS
1, as on Earth

tasks.title: A broken processor
tasks.situation: The station's urine-processing unit breaks down and cannot be fixed for a month. What will that mean for the water supply?

options.text: Much more water will have to be delivered by cargo ships.
Little change — most of the water comes from cargo ships anyway.
The crew will collect water from outside the station.

tasks.title: Where to point the camera
tasks.situation: At sunset on Mars, where in the sky should you point your camera to capture the blue light?

options.text: Toward the setting Sun — the blue glows around it.
Anywhere — the whole sky turns blue.
Straight up, away from the Sun.

tasks.title: A different power source
tasks.situation: Your base on Mars runs on a nuclear generator instead of solar panels. How dangerous is a planet-wide dust storm for its power supply?

options.text: Hardly at all — the danger was dust blocking sunlight, and wind on Mars is too weak to do damage.
Very — winds that strong could knock the equipment over.
Very — the storm will make the habitat lose air pressure.

tasks.title: How long until you hear it
tasks.situation: On Mars, you see a boulder crash down a slope 480 meters away. About how long after seeing it will you hear it?

options.text: About 2 seconds
About 1.4 seconds, as on Earth
You will not hear it at all — there is no air on Mars.

tasks.title: Asking for advice
tasks.situation: Mars and Earth are at their closest. You radio mission control a question and wait for the answer. What is the shortest time before the answer can arrive?

options.text: About 6 minutes — the message travels both ways.
About 3 minutes.
A second or two.
